name: Acetyl hexapeptide-3
lead: Acetyl hexapeptide-3 is the earlier name for the cosmetic peptide now listed under the INCI name acetyl hexapeptide-8 and sold as Argireline. It is a six-amino-acid fragment (Ac-Glu-Glu-Met-Gln-Arg-Arg-NH2) of SNAP-25, a protein involved in neurotransmitter release [1][2]. Wikipedia notes that the "-3" name is considered incorrect for this peptide [1].

It is marketed as a topical alternative to botulinum toxin for expression lines. It is proposed to interfere with SNARE complex formation and so dampen muscle contraction [1]. Wikipedia states that no dedicated double-blind trials of its wrinkle efficacy were available and that results across studies are inconsistent [1]. Its large, hydrophilic structure limits skin penetration, prompting microneedle and iontophoresis research [3][4].

paras: The peptide mimics the N-terminal region of SNAP-25 and is proposed to compete for a place in the SNARE complex, reducing vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release at the neuromuscular junction [1][2]. No clinical study has compared it directly with botulinum toxin, and the effective concentration is unclear [1].

Researchers describe poor skin permeation due to molecular weight and hydrophilicity; a 2015 study cited by Wikipedia found under 0.2% reached the outer skin layer after 24 hours [1]. Experimental microneedle patches, microneedle pretreatment and iontophoresis have been studied to improve delivery [3][4].

Wikipedia reports availability since 2001 and a 2002 paper introducing it as an anti-wrinkle peptide [1]. Grokipedia (AI-generated) attributes its development to the Barcelona company Lipotec, later part of Lubrizol [2].

A 2017 randomized study of 24 volunteers tested acetyl hexapeptide-3 alone and with tripeptide-10 citrulline over 60 days; the authors reported antiwrinkle activity and reduced transepidermal water loss for acetyl hexapeptide-3 [5]. Registered trials include a phase 3 study of periorbital wrinkles (n=70) and studies of acetyl hexapeptide-8 in blepharospasm, one terminated [6][7][8]. Wikipedia describes a 2012 pilot in blepharospasm in which the cream with botulinum toxin prolonged relief versus placebo [1]. Laboratory work on fibroblasts has also tested it in peptide mixtures [9].
Wikipedia reports a 2012 study with no significant adverse effects and a later review reporting no serious adverse events [1].

card.summary: The older name for Argireline, the topical 'Botox-alternative' peptide with modest, inconsistent evidence.
card.note: Poor skin penetration; no direct comparison with botulinum toxin.

quick.overview:
Acetyl hexapeptide-3 is the older name of Argireline (acetyl hexapeptide-8), a cosmetic peptide marketed as a topical alternative to botulinum toxin for expression lines.

Studies suggest it may improve the look of wrinkles, but results are inconsistent and hard to compare.
quick.mechanism: It copies a fragment of SNAP-25 and is proposed to interfere with the SNARE complex that triggers muscle-activating neurotransmitter release. Its poor skin absorption is an active research topic.
quick.risks: Reported adverse effects in the cited studies were minimal. It is a cosmetic ingredient sold over the counter.
